title: Class 6 Maths Fractions: Types, Number Line, Compare, Add & Subtract + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Fractions: NCERT Chapter Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: Class 6 maths fractions made clear: proper, improper, mixed, equivalent, number line, comparing and add-subtract, with a worked case study and a free quiz.
excerpt: Half a roti, three-quarters of a chapter done, one-and-a-half hours of study — fractions are everywhere in a Class 6 child’s day. Here is the whole NCERT chapter explained plainly, with a real-life case study and an 8-question quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Cut a roti into 4 equal pieces, eat 3, and you have just done Class 6 maths fractions without opening a book — you ate three-quarters, or 3/4. The NCERT Class 6 ‘Fractions’ chapter takes that everyday idea and gives it structure: what the parts are called, how to draw them on a number line, how to tell which fraction is bigger, and how to add and subtract them. Most children already feel fractions from sharing food and time. The chapter’s job is to turn that feel into clean, reliable arithmetic.

The word that unlocks the whole topic is equal. A fraction only makes sense when the whole is split into equal parts. Three unequal chunks of a chocolate bar are not thirds. I have watched sharp Class 6 students lose marks purely because they forgot that one word, so I put it first.

The parts of a fraction

Every fraction has a numerator (top) and a denominator (bottom). The denominator tells you how many equal parts the whole is cut into; the numerator tells you how many of those parts you took. In 3/4, the denominator 4 says ‘four equal parts’ and the numerator 3 says ‘we have three of them’. That is the entire idea. Everything else in the chapter is built on it.

Types of fractions in Class 6 maths

NCERT groups fractions into a handful of named types. Knowing the vocabulary is half the battle, because exam questions ask for it directly.

  • Proper fraction — numerator smaller than denominator, so its value is less than 1. Example: 2/5.
  • Improper fraction — numerator equal to or bigger than denominator, so its value is 1 or more. Example: 7/4.
  • Mixed fraction — a whole number and a proper fraction together, like 1¾. Every improper fraction can be written as a mixed one: 7/4 = 1¾.
  • Like fractions — same denominator, such as 2/7 and 5/7.
  • Unlike fractions — different denominators, such as 2/3 and 3/5.
  • Equivalent fractions — different numbers, same value: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number and the value never changes.

Turning improper into mixed (and back)

To write 11/4 as a mixed fraction, divide 11 by 4: it goes 2 times with 3 left over, so 11/4 = 2¾. To go back, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator: 2¾ = (2×4 + 3)/4 = 11/4. Both directions come up in the same exercise, so practise them as a pair.

Fractions on the number line

Drawing a fraction is the step most children skip and most exams reward. To place 3/5 on a number line, mark 0 and 1, then split that gap into 5 equal parts. Count 3 parts from 0 — that point is 3/5. For an improper fraction like 7/5, keep the same fifth-sized steps and count past 1: seven steps land you between 1 and 2, at 1⅖. The number line also shows equivalence beautifully: 1/2 and 2/4 land on exactly the same spot, which is far more convincing than any rule.

Comparing fractions

Two quick cases, then the general one:

SituationRuleExample
Same denominator (like)Bigger numerator wins5/8 > 3/8
Same numeratorSmaller denominator wins3/4 > 3/7
Unlike fractionsMake denominators equal (LCM), then compare2/3 vs 3/5

For 2/3 and 3/5, the LCM of 3 and 5 is 15. Rewrite as 10/15 and 9/15. Now they are like fractions, and 10/15 > 9/15, so 2/3 is the bigger one. The ‘same numerator’ rule is the counter-intuitive one worth stressing: with equal tops, a bigger bottom means the whole was cut into more, smaller pieces, so each piece is smaller.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Like fractions are easy: keep the denominator, add or subtract the numerators. So 2/9 + 5/9 = 7/9, and 5/9 − 2/9 = 3/9, which simplifies to 1/3. Always simplify the answer — NCERT expects the lowest form.

Unlike fractions need one extra step: make the denominators the same using their LCM, then add. For 1/4 + 1/6, the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. Rewrite as 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12. For mixed fractions, add the whole numbers and the fraction parts separately: 1½ + 2¼ = 3 + (2/4 + 1/4) = 3¾.

Case study: sharing a pizza and the study timetable

Here is the kind of passage the case-study e-book is built around. Read it, then solve.

Aarav orders one pizza cut into 8 equal slices for himself and his sister Diya. Aarav eats 3 slices and Diya eats 2 slices. Later that evening Aarav studies maths for 3/4 of an hour and science for 1/2 an hour.

  • What fraction of the pizza did Aarav eat? 3 slices out of 8, so 3/8.
  • What fraction did the two of them eat together? 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8 (like fractions, so just add the tops).
  • What fraction of the pizza was left? The whole is 8/8, so 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 remained.
  • How long did Aarav study in total? 3/4 + 1/2. The LCM of 4 and 2 is 4, so 3/4 + 2/4 = 5/4 = 1¼ hours.

Notice how one short story tested four separate skills — naming a fraction, adding like fractions, subtracting from a whole, and adding unlike fractions. That is exactly why case studies are such honest practice: they force the child to decide which rule applies, not just follow instructions.

A second quick case study

Meera’s water bottle holds 1 litre. She drinks 1/3 of it before school and 2/5 of it during school. How much has she drunk? Add 1/3 + 2/5. The LCM of 3 and 5 is 15, so 5/15 + 6/15 = 11/15 of the bottle. What is left? 15/15 − 11/15 = 4/15 litre. Same four-step thinking, brand-new context — that transfer is the goal.

quiz.title: Class 6 Maths Fractions Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions across the whole chapter — types of fractions, the number line, comparing, and adding and subtracting. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which of these is a proper fraction?
questions.explanation: A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator, so its value is less than 1. Only 3/8 fits.
11 divided by 4 is 2 with remainder 3, so 11/4 = 2¾.
Multiply top and bottom of 1/2 by 4 to get 4/8. The value stays the same.

questions.q: On a number line split into fifths, where does 7/5 lie?
questions.explanation: Seven fifth-sized steps from 0 pass 1 (which is 5/5) and land at 1⅖, between 1 and 2.
Same numerator, so the smaller denominator wins. Fourths are bigger pieces than sevenths, so 3/4 is greater.
Like fractions: keep the denominator and add the numerators. 2 + 5 = 7, so 7/9.
The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. Rewrite as 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.

questions.q: A cake is cut into 8 equal slices. If 5 are eaten, what fraction is left?
questions.explanation: The whole is 8/8. Subtract the 5 eaten: 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 remaining.

faq.q: What topics are in the Class 6 maths fractions chapter?
faq.a: The NCERT chapter covers types of fractions (proper, improper, mixed, like, unlike and equivalent), showing fractions on a number line, comparing fractions, and adding and subtracting both like and unlike fractions.

faq.q: What is the difference between an improper and a mixed fraction?
faq.a: An improper fraction has a numerator equal to or larger than its denominator, like 7/4. A mixed fraction writes the same value as a whole number plus a proper fraction, like 1¾. They are two ways of writing the same amount.

faq.q: How do you add fractions with different denominators?
faq.a: Find the LCM of the denominators, rewrite each fraction with that common denominator, then add the numerators. For 1/4 + 1/6 the LCM is 12, giving 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.

faq.q: How do you compare two unlike fractions?
faq.a: Convert them to like fractions using the LCM of the denominators, then the one with the bigger numerator is larger. For 2/3 and 3/5, both become fifteenths: 10/15 and 9/15, so 2/3 is greater.
